doc.title: Tom Baker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Trumpet, braces, euphonium, tuba and learning saxophone
summary: He took up trumpet in high school, switched to euphonium because of braces, then picked up tuba and, while recovering from a hernia, saxophone.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: But what was the next instrument after the piano?

It was the trumpet. And that was in high school. Well what do you have four years in high school? The fourth year I bought a trumpet or a cornet and got into the band. I’d been in the choir for four years, so I had ear training and I could read music, and I knew where I was supposed to be in the choir and all that, but playing the trumpet in the band was a lot of fun, especially marching. I loved marching in a band on the street — Sousa marches around the town and on the football field. That was a lot of fun. And then when I got into college, into junior college, my parents decided that my teeth stuck out too much, like a beaver. So I had to have braces on my teeth, which is — have you ever tried playing trumpet with braces on your teeth?

Yeah. It’s awful really. So I had to go into euphonium, which is a bigger mouthpiece. And for a couple of years I went off the trumpet. And then, about that time, we moved to Australia, and the braces came off. So I started playing the real stuff.
Is it a trick to go from one to the other? Physically?

Not for me. Not now. Now playing more than one instrument, my first other instrument besides the trumpet was the tuba. And I remember being in a band one night where the trombone player was doubling on sousaphone, on tuba. And when he went on to the trombone, nobody was playing the tuba. And I thought well, I asked the leader, is it okay, can I try this? And he says yeah — because it’s just like a trumpet. You blow in it, it’s got three valves, and at first it was a little weird but it took a couple of songs and then I learned you’ve got to relax your mouth, and then I got the notes. And it wasn’t that hard. So the tuba, that was the next one, and if we’re talking about some sort of chronology, the next instrument was the saxophone. And I was in England touring around and I was playing away and I felt this banging down here. And it was actually a hernia starting. And it got a little bit worse, and when I got back to Australia they said oh you’ll have to have that operated on. So I did, and for two or three months after that it was really impossible to play the trumpet at first.
Too much oomph down here? Too much pressure?

Yeah. Well hernias, as well as other things, are congenital. In other words you inherit them from you parents, and my father had hernias too, and so does my brother. So now I’ve had two hernias and it just happen to happen while I was playing the trumpet. But while knitting up, while I’ve got the stitches there, you don’t want to have any comedians around the house, you don’t have any of the usual guys that come around and tell you © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

jokes, because you don’t want to laugh, and you’re careful not to cough or anything else. And playing the trumpet was definitely out. But saxophone you could play a little bit, in the end blow and work the fingers. So while I was convalescing I learned the saxophone.
You just went out and picked up a saxophone?
Yeah. A friend of mine was going overseas and I said leave it with me and I’ll have a go, I’ve got to play something while you’re gone.
